utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick is a specialist in international law, and Mr. Fenrick, he works here in the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his job is here in the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he does here exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when and how this report was finalised?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the report was actually -- was finalised during the mission period. It wasn't finalised afterwards. I mean, we worked on the report to get it done before the team split up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this report was submitted to the UN Security Council?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard later that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this International Tribunal was established based on that report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the reports of the commission, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Inter alia, based on the report of that commission. May I have your answer.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Tribunal was the follow-up to the work of the commission of experts on the various reports which they -- they prepared on war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How objective were you in your work on the UN Security Council commission of experts?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to be objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything in your report about this in the sense of information that you obtained from any other side which is not the Croatian side and refers to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most -- I think nearly all the documents we obtained were obtained in Dubrovnik, which is on the Croatian side. I can't remember just offhand if there were other documents that we obtained from the international community, for example, the ECMM. I think we maybe went through Zagreb and were looking for documents from them. And I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you feel still today that your report is objective and balanced when, for instance, you see evidence of combat operations by the Croatian side from the immediate vicinity of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm -- let me just say I'm an historian. I know when you're that close to events you're not going to have a complete picture. The complete picture can only build up over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, sir, do you perhaps see things differently in relation to the way you saw things in 1993 regarding, of course, events which are under review?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you've probably seen a few examples of how I've had doubts about things over the years. There was a long discussion about boats. I've learned recently some information that I did not know about. That certainly enriches the picture of what was going on in Dubrovnik at the time. And what I'm saying is this information fills out things. If you're -- I think you're also asking does that change fundamentally my vision of the past. And the answer to that is that it doesn't change fundamentally that vision of the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who gave you this information that actually complemented your vision of events in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first place, Mr. Stevens, the investigator who came in 2001 and mentioned the question of the mortars in the park. Secondly, well, yourself, sir. You've mentioned some things about the HOS. You've added information to the information that I have already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any other information from anybody else? Did you actually actively seek such information?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't actually seeking information on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear of any other military positions apart from those that you referred to yesterday; the Croatian positions, that is, in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a position on Srdj. There is a position on Hotel Belvedere. And there was a great big wooded area in Lapad. There could have perhaps been positions there. There were positions in the inlet, west of the town. There were front -- there were front lines. There were front positions. But it's not the Rijeka Dubrovacka. It's the Mokosica and those places. I know that there were positions there, or I had heard that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From whom did you learn this information after this period that we're talking about, 1991, 1992, and 1993, if these people are not Mr. Stevens or I myself?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What I was talking about, those positions, the positions I'm referring to, in fact, at the time of the mission. I haven't heard about -- I haven't heard specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear of the Gradac park?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recognise the name of that park.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll be coming to that later, but I will revert to the report now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher to show the witness this document, please, and of course provide a copy to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, is this the report that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it say on the top "United Nations Security Council" on page 1? Please have a look at page 1.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, is there the exact number and the exact indication mark of that report as is usual within the system employed in the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please let us now take a look at some of the parts of the report, some parts, rather, of this report which are of relevance. Please take a look at page number 4 of the report. And take a look at the third full paragraph on page 4. Please peruse it and then we'll discuss it briefly. Actually, the second full paragraph on page 4. [In English] "The commission was provided with ..." You see?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Okay. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that the essential information for the compiling of this report was inaccessible to you and your colleagues at the time that we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear from this paragraph that a lot of relevant information was not available, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you didn't get anything in the way of information from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia which related to the establishment of units, the locations, and the movement of military forces in and around Dubrovnik in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear from this paragraph that there was no such information forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in this report you note that that is the greatest shortcoming, this unavailability of such information, namely?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to some specific part of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring at all times to this particular paragraph. I just want to hear you say whether this is so or not, because this is the introductory part, and it obviously is in the section of report which is marked B, which is the methodology in the report. It is a part of the report, in other words.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The report says it was the most notable gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Republic of Croatia, the highest levels of the Republic of Croatia, had promised to you that you would obtain the information that you needed in order to fill that gap?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't remember if that promise was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll take a look at this. At line number 5, for instance: [In English] "This is how access to important sources of information was effectively denied even though the commission had previously visited all the key local government officials and secured their promise of positive support for the commission's investigative efforts."

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's mentioned the commission visited. This may have been upstream -- I don't remember having such discussions. The commission visited. We were part of a team that was sent down to Dubrovnik. I assume there were other discussions. If they had written this, it's certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at page number 5 of this report. The first full paragraph after this enumeration, following the letters of the alphabet. Which starts with ... [In English] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have your comment on it. In relation to this paragraph or is it self-explanatory, in your view?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's fairly straightforward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at page number 7 of this report. Section 3, where it says ... [In English] [Previous translation continues]... [Interpretation] And then the second paragraph again. Is it correct that your commission noted that free elections in the Republic of Croatia had brought chauvinist nationalists, Franjo Tudjman's nationalists to power?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written there that the elections brought to power nationalist parties such as the HDZ in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that true? Is that exactly what I said? Do you share this conviction?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said chauvinist. I mean, the adjective used is "nationalist."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I used exactly the terminology "nationalist party," which is used here.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were nationalist parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And are they a chauvinist party?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: National parties aren't exactly chauvinists parties, necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is the HDZ or was the HDZ an example of a nationalist party of chauvinist orientation?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be qualified as a hard-line nationalist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From which it is just one step to chauvinism. Do you not agree with me?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Chauvinism" is not a word I use quite often. I'm not sure what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us not belabour that point. Please take a look at page number 8, the first paragraph. "JNA garrisons blockaded by Croatian forces ..."

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you want me to read this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. It's very brief. Does it just note -- it just notes that the garrisons were blockaded by the Croatian side. Do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look at page number 9, section C marked ... [In English] [Previous translation continues].... Take a look at paragraph number 4 on page 9 as part of this section, and please read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it say as a conclusion that the commander of the JNA sector in and around Dubrovnik was a vice admiral by rank?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No other name is mentioned in respect of the sector commander there; right?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear about Admiral Jokic, Vice Admiral Miodrag Jokic?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that name. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether he perhaps was the commander of that sector holding the rank of vice admiral who is referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was it that you heard about General Pavle Strugar for the first time?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these -- when was it? These were names that sort of came up. I can't remember when I heard it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But surely you heard about it after the period in which this report was drawn up.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about it, of course, recently with the indictment that was handed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This same page, please. Section 5. This reiterates a statement that you were denied -- your commission was denied access to key information during that period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at page number 10 in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If I may once again. The way my learned friend phrased the question was, "this reiterates that you were denied" access, it should be. I take objection with the word "reiterate" because the first time it was mentioned it was denied access held by the Republic of Croatia. This time round, however, it's the lack of information from Croatian and Serbian military sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I even need say this, because at the beginning, the witness said that he got nothing from the JNA. He neither asked nor received any information from them, if you remember. So I don't see why this should be raised as a question. But of course, the report is quite clear itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at page 10. So the second full paragraph, the first sentence, which starts with --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Without information"; right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you read this sentence for us, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Without information on the marginal activities to the ad hoc military units formed in Croatia to resist the JNA advance, the determination of what constituted a valid military objective for JNA attention is very difficult."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that you didn't have valid information that could serve for the drawing of conclusions as to what the activities were of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly; military operations outside the town would certainly fall into that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain now to me how you came by this particular explanation, military operations outside the town? How did this cross your mind? Did you know that at the time? How did you come up with that particular explanation at this particular moment when I posed this question to you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the picture -- the picture of military operations throughout the commune is something that's not very clear. I don't know very much about it. If we were talking about the shellings of Dubrovnik, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is there such an explanation or such a conclusion in this report? How do you arrive at this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not deriving the -- I'm not deriving the conclusion from the report. By the way, I have not seen this document in a very, very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But do you know if there is a conclusion to that effect anywhere in the report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what we've seen so far today, we've seen that there has been a lot of information which has been denied to this -- to the commission of experts, a lot of military information from both sides. And that's one question that's very, very, important. About operations, the chain of command. My reference is to, simply, the question of damage done by shelling, that's all, in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have the normal break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, will you please look at page 13 of this document that we've just been dealing with. In Section C of this on that page, look at paragraph 4. So subsection C, para 4. Did the experts' commission at the moment when this report was being filed stress that the shelling was probably from JNA positions, without any certainty about the claim? The word "probably" indicates that it's only a possibility.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A strong possibility. Look at page 14, the second paragraph. Will you please read out the first two sentences in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On November -- 7th of November, 1991, an ultimatum was announced on the local radio demanding that all Croatian forces surrender by noon. On 8th of November, 1991, Vice Admiral Jokic announced that discussions with the Croats had not succeeded and that he would spare only the Old Town."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would be correct in concluding that this ultimatum of the 7th of November would be an ultimatum made by Admiral Jokic, according to this report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It with appear to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it also say that Jokic said that "he" would spare the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it written.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would that be reflective of the fact that it was a conclusion of the commission that Jokic was in command, in charge, in the area in question?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't necessarily conclude that he was in charge. He was just the chap who had announced that the discussions had not succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It says here that "he would spare the Old Town." "He would spare only the Old Town." Does that seem to indicate that he was the person who was able to decide whether or not to spare it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could be the person. It could be, simply, a rather personalised rhetorical device.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Questions of command and who was in command, in my submission, is a legal question which will be determined by the Trial Chamber at the end of the day. Questions of command can be analysed on a de facto basis and on a de jure basis. The witness has given his answer. I would request that Mr. Petrovic do not stray into asking the witness questions of legal import.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, certainly the factual foundation which you have pursued is very properly put forward and including the fact that there was an apparent statement by a person other than the accused who was apparently exercising the position of command. You've got that. To go on then and try and have this witness reach some conjectural conclusion is going too far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, Mr. Kaiser, does the report submitted to the UN Security Council ever mention the preliminary report done by the institute from Dubrovnik that we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I mentioned to you I haven't seen this document in a very long time, and I can't really answer that until I see the document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. It isn't mentioned, but we'll deal with that later. Please look at page 16, the bottom of page 16 where it says: "The inquiry of the JNA," and the first paragraph of page 16. Read it and then I will ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it clear from this passage that in relation to the events of the 6th of December the processes against these events were made from the highest level of the international community?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it follow therefrom that the protests were directed primarily at the federal authorities in Belgrade in view of the level from which the protests were made regarding the events of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that the European Union made a protest on the same day according to what it says in this report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it mentioned specifically the ECMM who made the protest, which is an emanation of the European Union, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Yugoslav People's Army had promised a full investigation regarding the incident?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the information which these -- the team of experts and the commission found proper to write here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the same text, further down below, it says that "On the 7th of December, a delegation of the JNA visited the Old Town to investigate the damage"?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please look at only one more paragraph, para 3 on the same page. The first sentence. Will you read it out for us.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the perspective of the law of armed conflict, it is clear that there were valid military objectives in and around the city of Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, up until now the witness has not read out aloud sections of the report which currently is not before Your Honours as an exhibit and has not been tendered. I don't know whether my learned friend intends to ask for the exhibit to be tendered. However, my observation on the passage that has been read out is that it is a matter of pure legal import, so I would object to it on that ground. And I object, furthermore, to parts of the report being read out if it is not going to be tendered at the end of the day. I have my own submissions to make on tendering the report but I'll leave that until Mr. Petrovic announces whether or not he intends to submit the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence proposes and requests that this be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to do this at the end of my cross-examination, but if it's necessary I'll do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this particular matter, an expression involving gooses and ganders springs to mind, perhaps put more eloquently by Your Honour as reciprocity. Dr. Kaiser in this matter is a co-author of the commission of experts' report and to the extent that this report would be submitted, I would also submit that the exhibit currently marked as P51 MFI should also be submitted along the same grounds. I would request Mr. Petrovic perhaps to stipulate on what legal basis he requests to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Your Honour. I'll be happy to. First of all, it is a report which is a fundamental document of the institution in which we all find ourselves today. It was based on this report that the ICTY was founded. It is the first point, all not the most important. Second, the gentleman who is testifying here today is the co-author of this document, as my learned friend so correctly observed; co-author. It is precisely the fact upon which the Defence insists, speaking of the unfortunate preliminary report. He is the co-author to the UN Security Council, and the preliminary report is something from which he distances himself. He hasn't even read it, because it is not written in a language he understands; and I can, if necessary, provide as many arguments as necessary. And I will provide them when my learned friend asks to tender P51. But to look for similarity between those two documents is absolutely inappropriate. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I perhaps spoke a bit too quickly. If I look at the front page of the item which my learned friend submitted to me and to the witness, Dr. Kaiser's role is defined as consultant to the commission of experts which is exactly the same role he was granted with respect to P51 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment, Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- I find it difficult to distinguish this document from P51. While it may be speaking in its contents in some respects to matters that are relevant to this prosecution, it is speaking as the product of a committee of inquiry that looked at these matters on its face in a very hasty way in 1993 with nowhere near the resources that would be appropriate to a full investigation of all the relevant circumstances, and with a very different objective and purpose from that which faces this Chamber. I could speak at greater length, but that is sufficient to indicate that the report is not obviously a document of direct relevance to the Chamber. Now, some aspects of it may have a relevance because of their bearing on the evidence of this particular witness, and I have been assuming that that is the basis upon which you were dealing with this report in your cross-examination. But this Chamber at the moment could hardly rely on this report or the contents of it as proof of any of the matters that it has to consider in this trial, whether proof for the Prosecution or for the Defence, because there is such limited authentication of it and such limited reliance that on the face of it could be placed upon any conclusions that are set out in it. I do accept that there is a fairly strong parallel between this report and P51, and it may be at the end of the day that whatever happens to P51 will happen to this report, at least in part to maintain an even balance one way or the other between Prosecution and Defence. But at the moment, I would think the report not directly or obviously admissible, particularly given the role of the present witness in its preparation and the nature of the process which led to its preparation. For that reason, it would be preferable if your cross-examination did not extend to a detailed reading into the transcript of passages from it. You certainly may well want to direct the attention of the witness to particular passages and learn whether he had a role in the inclusion of that part or whether he agrees with what is there said or whether he has a different understanding of that matter, and so on. And I don't want to suggest that what I've just said is exhaustive of the relevance and of the use you may make of the report, but I think it would be prudent for the moment not to be reading very significant extracts from the report into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for the comments and remarks you made. At this moment, the Defence shall for the time being abandon its request to exhibit this document and, therefore, there is no need to discuss the matter further at today's hearing. The issue is, therefore, moot. And I will not deal with the report any more. Instead, I should ask the witness to look at exhibit P62, specifically tab 3. Mr. Kaiser, I should like us to deal now with document under tab 3 of Exhibit P62. And in this context, would you kindly look at page 8. Page 8 of this report in its English version -- sorry, page 8 of the document, not the report. And before that, would you kindly explain to the Chamber the import of the zone located directly next to the ramparts of the Old Town, abutting the ramparts.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned that I had discovered very recently that there had been what looks to be an extension of the core -- yes -- no. Zone immediate du noyau monumental du Dubrovnik. This could be a buffer zone. It's called a buffer zone. But I'm sorry, I never really looked at this document. May I just look at it briefly to see exactly what it is, if it's an extension or simply a definition of the buffer zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. We have not reached the buffer zone yet. I'm asking you what the import is of the zone in this document related to the 95 bis, the extended zone abutting the Old Town established by the document before you, Exhibit P62, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's my question.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the buffer zone.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, we're talking about an extension of the Old Town itself. Annex 16 of our report, as Mr. Carnez and I indicated, raised some questions about the delimitation of the Old Town. There were things that were not clear to us, and we felt that these sorts of things had to be clarified, where the limits of the Old Town where were. Now, there was a very important element. As I said earlier, a few days ago now, there were various structures, various buildings, fortifications or buildings of economic importance which were part of the economic and military structure of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, and it's very logical that the town be taken -- be considered as a whole. And if I understand, this was the response which was made by the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, to ask for the extension of the World Heritage Site to the Old Town. We also had the problem of the Kasa [phoen], with the breakwater. This means that this area is part of the Old Town, which means that it has to be managed the same way as the Old Town. There are all sorts of restrictions with what can be done to buildings. It's that sort of matter. And this would protect these buildings also. For example, these quarantine buildings, it would protect them from significant changes. This is what this would be about. This would be the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, in terms of cultural and historical importance of the Old Town, the importance of this zone is also very high, and these two zones cannot be artificially separated. They are part of one and the same cultural and historical whole. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at this same page 8 which I asked you to open. The last sentence in paragraph B. The English version of the report. Do you have the English or the French in front you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the French in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't know if they coincide. Would you please check.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last sentence goes like: "In the course of this process was prepared technical documentation," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I could have your indulgence for a moment. I apologise for this delay, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, I really regret it, but I couldn't find the paper I needed. Did you find what I asked you to? The description of inventory. That's a sub-heading, page 8 of the English translation, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Description of Inventory" is what it is. Is that what it is? Okay. I'll look for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I may be of some assistance. It's page 9 in the French version. It's page 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, b is the "History of Preservation and Conservation" and c is the "Means of Preservation and Conservation" and the management plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This will probably be the quickest way to proceed. If I may ask the assistance of -- just a moment. I need to locate it.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have page 6, "Description and Inventory", b.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So under b, "Description and Inventory". Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, have you found the item I mentioned? Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have a heading small b, "Description and Inventory."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. That's precisely what I would like to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, I'm interested in the last sentence, the description of borders, of the borders of this zone in question.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the border on the west is Gradac park, then Don Frana Bulica Street, Ante Starcevic Street, Iza Grada Street until the Fran Supila Street at the end. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you now please look at page -- in fact, it's a map in the same section, a little before the page we looked at, 03245807 being the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made photocopies to facilitate our work. I hope it's not a problem to distribute it. You will now receive a copy of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, these little dots you see there are indications of the border of the zone in question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see on the right-hand side just next to this border, do you see the mark "Gradac"?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Gradac is?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen earlier that it's a park.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can I then please ask you to mark on this copy which is in front of you using the highlighter, just encircle this word, "Gradac," which I would like to offer, Your Honour. Put it on the ELMO so we can look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Your Honour, for your ease of orientation, I should like to tender this document as evidence, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please speak into the microphone. The interpreter cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the marked document please be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. admitted to the file as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And while that is occurring, I think it should be done that we mark for identification the United Nations Security Council report that was so much the subject of cross-examination so that we have a document in the record that is identified and identifiable, should it later become an exhibit. So that will be given a marked-for-identification number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be numbered Defence Exhibit D29, and the report will be marked for identification MFI D30.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown this photograph which was taken from this film, from this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a photograph taken from the film which the witness who testified before this Chamber submitted to the OTP, and the OTP submitted it to the Defence team. Mr. Kaiser, can you tell us what is it that you see on this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge of events in and around Dubrovnik, the fact that -- is this changed in any way by the fact that you can see that this kind of weaponry was deployed in this zone?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before the witness answers that question, I would just like to state that I don't know whether my learned friend intends on tendering this particular photograph, but there does not appear to be any date on the photograph itself. I would have thought that before the witness were asked to give an answer to that particular question he should at least know to which date this photograph is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you help us with that, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, I cannot, unfortunately, Your Honours. I can help you just by saying that this photograph was taken in October, November, or December 1991. I can help you to that extent. And that was according to the evidence which was given to the OTP by the witness Grbic, and the OTP of course gave it to us. I'm not asking Mr. Kaiser to say anything about the specific date. What I'm asking him is what his reaction is that at the very boundary of the protected zone we have this artillery piece which was photographed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Yes, Dr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's presumably on the boundary of the protected zone, which is protected later on. If this is indeed a photograph taken between October and December 1991, this is something I haven't seen before, and I haven't heard about it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If this photograph is authentic, would something of this kind cause your deepest concern about the protected zone of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Now we have to get this chronology also straight. This change in the boundary is carried out later on. So if this piece is there between October and December, it is indeed outside of the boundary of the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is the extended protected zone, as you said before a while ago, was it equally valuable in 1950 [as interpreted], 1991, and 1994? Can we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protected zone -- the protected zone is a protected zone, and it is equally valuable. But it also depends on when it's protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does the content of that zone, irrespective of when its form of protection began, does the content of that zone, is it something which is very valuable property irrespective of the actual commencement of the formal protection regime? Is it -- does it have equal status in 1991 and in 1995 or did something happen to make that valuable only in 1995, something which fundamentally changed the zone? Did its essence of a highly valuable cultural and artistic zone exist always?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about two different kinds of value. I mean, you have a recognised legal protection, and you also then have a cultural value. There are two different things. The legal protection is supposed to, as much as it's possible, to cover things which are of culturally valued. But there is a difference. We're talking about legal protection, and we're talking about cultural value.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this zone immediately next to the Gradac park, was it a zone of the highest cultural value also in 1991, the same value of the Old Town? No? As you said a while ago.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't have the same legal value. It would have a different cultural value because it was not inside of the walls, but it would be considered part of the town system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Today, is today the Gradac park protected in the same way as the world cultural heritage is, as a part of the world's cultural heritage as park Stradun, as the Stradun Street is because of its cultural and historical value?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as it would be outside of the zone of the World Heritage Site, it would not enjoy exactly the same protection as the World Heritage Site. If it is listed "heritage" under a register, a national register of heritage, it would have the right to a certain level of protection. It might not be the same -- probably would not be exactly the same level as for the World Heritage Site itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, I'm asking you about today. Is the zone today the zone that is under review and the zone which is marked on the map which you encircled a while ago, which shows its boundary, is its legal status today the same as the status of Stradun -- at this point in time today? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gradac is outside of the zone. Therefore, its legal status is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So is the boundary and the area right next to the boundary -- five metres away, that is -- is that today protected just like Stradun is?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the zone five metres away from Gradac, was it from the cultural and historical standpoint equally valuable in 1991 as it is today?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When it is protected --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: -- like the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... concluded, it recognised its historic value that it didn't have under the legal classification in 1991, but it recognises it in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the zone was formalised as such in 1991, but its essential cultural and historical value existed also in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter corrects herself. The first year is 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It had the same value.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes or no. Thank you. We didn't have to use up this much time to establish this simple fact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please not overlap with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would you -- can I have this photograph which I just gave and the photograph which I offered yesterday which shows Minceta, could these two photographs be exhibited? And the Defence will attempt to provide colour photographs for you which we haven't been able to do up to this point, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, these photographs are taken out of a video which, as Mr. Petrovic rightly states, was a video supplied by the witness Grbic who has testified before the Tribunal. I'm always in favour of providing the evidence in its entirety if possible. So if Mr. Petrovic is seeking to admit the whole video, then that is agreeable as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that video not tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I don't believe it has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, which was the one which you mentioned from yesterday, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the photograph of Bogisic park and the photograph of Minceta. So I should like to ask that photograph about which our distinguish witness spoke yesterday, which I can see here is on the table in front of you. I would like that photograph and this photograph of today to be tendered as evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will each be separately received. And the video itself; is that to hand, Mr. Kaufman?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: It can be obtained. It my friend agrees, we can find it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could produce it as soon as convenient, and that will be received as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you just pause, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yesterday's photograph will be exhibited as Exhibit D31, and the photograph submitted today will be Exhibit D32.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, will you please explain to us what is the buffer zone in the light of the document which is P63, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, normally a buffer zone is a zone outside of the registered, inscribed zone of a historic monument or natural park or whatever. And buffer zone is also subject to certain protection, certain legal restrictions; on its use, on the buildings, on the changes, but it is a much, much lower -- needs a lower level of protection. And the exact servitudes have to be defined specifically by different countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look now at the map which is marked 03245801. That is its ERN number, which is in the right top corner.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put the map on the ELMO. Do you know Dubrovnik that well as to be able to tell me what the boundaries of this buffer zone are?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I can't tell you exactly what those boundaries are in terms of streets and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you just, geographically speaking, make this distinction? Like, say, this north part, where would this northern part be, approximately?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean it looks quite clearly, as it goes up to the limit, in fact, of the inhabited, built-up zones. That's what you would see on the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is Srdj, roughly?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be up here. Well, sorry. It would be up here, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're indicating a position off the map and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- and to the north?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this northern zone or this northern boundary is the highway? Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be a highway, yes, a big road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, do you know how far the Srdj peak is from that road? If you don't know exactly, can you make an approximation.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The peak from Srdj as the crow flies. Seven or 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe this map could be of use. Would you please -- would the witness please consult this map. Could you please juxtapose these two maps. And what do you think? How far is it from the Adriatic coastal road to Srdj?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you cannot assess it, then --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean from this map it look -- it would look a bit less. About 500 metres, 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. This will be ascertained in other ways. Let us not dwell on it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this map be marked possibly for identification or is Defence Exhibit for easier reference in the further course of our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be no objection. It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D33.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my only comment would be that it's not cartographically accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not out of keeping with much of what we have then, Mr. Kaufman. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say I'm surprised by the remark of my learned colleague, because it seems that the defence maps show that Srdj much closer to the Old Town than perhaps some would wish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you, Mr. Kaiser, move on to tab number 6. Your report, in other words, and locate in the report the section which is marked E1.1, entitled "Overview of the Detailed Survey of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments." And its number is 073357. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, but there seems to be a difference in numbers at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You have found it. I can see it from here. But you have found it in the French version, that is why. Tell me, please, these annotations that have been added there in your handwriting, are they, first of all, in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They seem to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain to us what it written there. What did you write it down and why?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no date on it. I can read it to you. It says "quality survey question by C. Kaiser, especially with" -- "with regard," I suppose, "to calibre of ordnance" [quote].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell me if you don't know when you wrote this, can you tell me why you wrote this?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote this afterwards. I don't know exactly when, but I wrote it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you write it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some doubts about the calibres that were indicated on this annex document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kinds of doubts did you have? What gave rise to these doubts? How did you come to the conclusion that there existed some problems in that regard?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't -- I think this had probably been if I had seen one or two of the -- or some of the entries in the report, the preliminary report, it would be on the -- probably on the basis of that where I question whether or not in fact the calibre was, in fact, the right calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So your doubt to the extent that there were mistakes in the report was engendered after your having perused one or two reports already.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My doubts came afterwards, probably after having had some access to some of the forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this section which is marked D2.1. In this section, you refer to the fact that JNA artillery had the intention to shell the Old Town for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's page 0303073354 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, where did this idea, this information come from, these three days of shelling?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a rumour that was sort of flying around at the time. In fact, it's indicated here. "One is tempted to say only historians can determine if the federal artillerymen had the intention to shell the Old Town for three days as it was said"; "as it was said."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what kind of importance do rumours have that they would deserve to be incorporated in a report which has very serious claims to objectivity? What place do rumours have in such a report? What need is there for comment on rumours?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, there are a lot of ideas that are floating around and they can keep floating around. The way it is described here is that only historians are going to know if this is the truth. That rumour may have disappeared totally from history, but at the time it was written, there was a rumour. What if people start repeating the rumour all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't see in your report anything that would, for instance, be a rumour that you heard from the other side. Why don't you report that to the General-Secretary? For instance, were are there no rumours about the use of mortars from the Old Town? Why don't you deal with that in your report? That, too, is a rumour, if what you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was about Dubrovnik and what was happening at Dubrovnik. You noticed in this report that there is nothing about the preliminary meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Look at section F, please, F1.1.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell me what your conclusions were here about the number of citizens in the Old Town, the population. Is it true that you claim that not more than 50 per cent of the population of the Old Town were actually residing in their own homes around the 6th of December, that under a half of them only were in their homes at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The passage -- the passage is implying that the population that was actually -- the population of the Old Town was between one-third and one-half.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th December; correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at the first paragraph above this section F. Here you say that the shooting was intentionally grouped on the parts of the Old Town lying on the embankments which had suffered significant damage from earthquakes in the 1970s. It is just above the sub-heading section 5. How did you come -- how did you arrive at this conclusion? Is this also a rumour?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this isn't a rumour, but this is a belief that I don't have any more. Now, let me try and explain it. There was an earthquake in 1979. The zone of the ground that is the most sensitive is the infill zone which is the Stradun, and south of the Stradun. This is most sensitive to the earthquake, and most earthquake damage was particular to this zone. When we looked at maps at the time, we looked at maps of the earthquake zone, and then we had the maps of the impacts and the damage on the Old Town, there was definitely an overlapping. A lot of the buildings that were badly damaged were located in this infill zone. And afterwards when we walked around, some buildings seemed to -- buildings that had not been properly repaired after the earthquake of 1979, the cracks seemed to have become enlarged. So the concern was that -- the question was, and it was answered a little bit perhaps too quickly -- in fact, it was targeting in this zone because this zone was the more fragile zone. Now, this was a hypothesis at the time. It was discussed. This was suggested by the people we were with in the institute. There were indeed a lot of cracks, but there were a lot of -- you know, it doesn't mean that those cracks were related to the earthquake damage. There were some that were. This was a hypothesis. Today I would say I don't think this is -- let's put it this way, it is the people, the real specialists, the architects and engineers who went to Dubrovnik and worked on the town afterwards did not say that this seemed to be going on or that these buildings were especially damaged because they had been situated on the earthquake zone. This is a hypothesis which should just be abandoned, but something was written in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To cut a long story short, you don't hold this belief any more, and this statement in the report is incorrect. But tell me, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't hold this belief any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, in that part of town, you just mentioned there were structures where the damage from earthquakes from 1970s was not repaired even. But tell me, how did the people who made this report distinguish between what can be qualified as a bad condition of the building due to the earthquake and the consequences of what may have happened on the 6th of December or perhaps in October, November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how they made the distinction, because you would have to go through the whole report and look at each form to see if there was an allusion made to earlier earthquake damage. For example, yesterday we came across the example of the synagogue which had been damaged in the 1979 earthquake and had not been -- it hadn't been properly repaired after the earthquake. I don't -- we'd have to go back and see what did they write. What did they write on the form, the damage form, for the synagogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that 99 per cent of the records that were made bear no reflection of any damage from the earthquake, does it mean that nobody made the distinction between earlier earthquake damage and damage inflicted in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be they may have -- I'm not sure what it means. They could have separated it out unconsciously -- no, consciously. I'm not sure what it means exactly. I'm not sure how they treated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, if in 99 per cent of the records there is no mention of the condition of structures prior or any description of damage that existed before, does it mean that they did not make any distinction because there is no trace of it, no written record? It doesn't say whether the crack is from an explosion or from an earthquake, or the crack resulted from the generally bad condition of the building.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some buildings were repaired after the earthquake, some weren't repaired. In this report, they were supposed to be looking specifically for damage which could be traced back, could be traced back to a projectile of some sort. Did -- the question you're asking, did they do that; did they successfully filter out the earlier damage, did they mix old cracks -- say that old cracks were in fact new cracks when they weren't? It's that kind of question that you're asking, and I can't give you the answer to that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you've had a big day, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Dr. Kaiser, tomorrow I must ask you to return. I can only say you're a day nearer the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the Trial Chamber does in fact adjourn, I would on behalf of the Victims and Witness Unit once again request, perhaps, to know how long Mr. Petrovic intends on continuing cross-examination, because we do have witnesses, of course, lined up waiting to give evidence at the conclusion of Dr. Kaiser's evidence. It would be helpful if we had an estimate of how long cross-examination is anticipated to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is very difficult for me to adjust what I think is important with the position of the Victims and Witnesses Unit. I think it is important for us to deal with important issues from this mountain of documents that the testimony of this witness relates to. It is the essence of the indictment against our client. To limit my questioning above what is absolutely necessary is not acceptable to us, but I will do it. And I have already skipped a great number of subjects, because the lack of logic and the abundance of discrepancies is something that we have to put forward -- although not entirely, because somehow or otherwise physically it is impossible -- and I am limiting myself only to vital things. But even in the present reduced form, I have to continue, although I will make further reductions to try to free Mr. Kaiser and let him go back to the obligations that he has abandoned in order to come here and testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Petrovic. We're grateful for that. Can I say that in view of the ground that you've covered and the time that you've spent and your hopes and expectations earlier today that the Chamber would hope that you would be able to conclude your cross-examination in the first session of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, Your Honour. Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will then adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.
